strengths: Well-designed dual-resolution architecture (DRSR) that solves the temporal mismatch between speech (25Hz) and text (~3Hz) modalities by running the LLM backbone at 5Hz while generating high-fidelity speech outputs through a Speech Refined Head (SRH).

The 'CoM-Mixing' training strategy is an effective curriculum learning approach that allows the model to leverage text as a reasoning scaffold (Chain-of-Modality) before emitting concurrent speech tokens.

Impressive experimental results, establishing a new state-of-the-art performance on spoken QA benchmarks (Llama Questions and Web Questions) compared to similarly sized models (such as GLM-4-Voice, Moshi, and VITA-Audio).
Significant training and inference efficiency gains, reducing GPU hour requirements by nearly 50% compared to standard 1x frame-rate configurations without sacrificing conversational accuracy.
weaknesses: Speech synthesis quality (as measured by UTMOS) is slightly lower (3.86) than competitive baselines like GLM-4-Voice (4.33) and Moshi (3.90), suggesting that token grouping and dual-resolution processing may slightly degrade the acoustic naturalness and fine-grained expressive details.

The evaluation is restricted to Spoken QA accuracy and does not quantitatively evaluate interactive spoken dialogue metrics like response generation latency, turn-taking capability, or emotion/prosody control, which are highlighted as major motivations in the introduction.

Details regarding the step-by-step alignment during the parallel autoregressive forward pass in Eq. (1) could be clearer, specifically how the 5Hz speech tokens and variable-rate text tokens are synchronized and processed in parallel at each step.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly relevant and timely topic in the field of spoken dialogue systems: the temporal resolution mismatch between high-rate speech representations and low-rate text tokens.

The proposed Dual-Resolution Speech Representation (DRSR) with a Speech Refined Head (SRH) is a logical approach to compress the input speech rate to 5Hz, thereby reducing the computational burden on the LLM core.

The authors conduct extensive comparative experiments on Spoken Question Answering benchmarks (Llama Questions and Web Questions) against a wide range of competitive baselines, achieving strong performance.

The paper provides comprehensive ablation studies (such as the impact of the grouping factor, continuous speech encoder, pre-training, and data scaling) which help clarify the impact of different components.
weaknesses: Conceptual Compromise on Parallel Real-Time Modeling: The proposed Chain-of-Modality (CoM) strategy is highly emphasized for improving performance. However, CoM prompts the model to first generate the text response completely before doing parallel speech-text generation. This sequential process is conceptually very close to standard cascaded or text-first pipelines (e.g., SpeechGPT), which significantly increases initial response latency and defeats the core advantage of simultaneous parallel modeling.

Lack of Generation Latency/RTF Evaluation: For any conversational or interactive voice agent, latency metrics (such as Real-Time Factor (RTF) or Time-to-First-Token (TTFT)) are critical. Although the paper shows training efficiency in GPU hours (Figure 2), it does not provide quantitative latency comparison of the inference phase, especially given that the SRH must run k autoregressive steps for every single step of the LLM.

Novelty and Architectural Distinction: The grouping and hierarchical decoding of audio tokens is conceptually similar to previous works like Moshi (which also uses a multi-stream/hierarchical setup) and Mini-Omni. The distinction between the proposed ungrouping + SRH mechanism and prior multi-token/hierarchical prediction heads needs to be more clearly articulated and theoretically justified.

Clarity and Mathematical Precision: In Section 3.2, Equation 3 defines the grouping of discrete tokens using a concatenation operator (||). Since $s_j$ are discrete token indices, concatenating them directly is mathematically incorrect; it should be performed on their respective embeddings. Additionally, several dimensional variables (such as $d_g$, $d_h$, $d_{text}$, $d_{ug}$) are introduced in Equations 3, 4, and 5 without clear definitions, making the exact architecture of the projection and splitting steps hard to reproduce.

Suboptimal Speech Naturalness: As shown in Table 3, the UTMOS score of DRVOICE (3.86) is noticeably lower than some of the baselines (such as GLM-4-Voice at 4.33). This indicates that the acoustic quality and naturalness of the generated speech still lag behind competitive state-of-the-art systems.

strengths: Innovative dual-resolution speech representation (DRSR) design that compresses the LLM input frame rate to 5Hz to align with text tokens, while leveraging a Speech Refined Head (SRH) to generate fine-grained speech tokens at 25Hz.

Highly efficient architecture that reduces computational costs significantly (achieving nearly 50% GPU hour savings compared to 1x grouping) while simultaneously improving speech-text understanding and generation performance.
Achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) results on competitive Spoken QA benchmarks (Llama Questions and Web Questions) compared to strong contemporary baselines such as Kimi-Audio and VITA-Audio.

Thorough ablation studies and scaling analysis that clearly justify the utility of each proposed component, including the continuous speech encoder, SRH pre-training, grouping factor, and the CoM-mixing training strategy.
weaknesses: Lack of quantitative latency and Real-Time Factor (RTF) measurements during inference. Although the 5Hz LLM rate reduces computational complexity, the SRH still requires $k$ sequential autoregressive passes per step. A detailed time-to-first-token (TTFT) and throughput comparison would strengthen the efficiency claims.

The speech naturalness and quality (UTMOS) of the proposed model is slightly lower than some baselines (e.g., GLM-4-Voice), likely due to the inherent speech synthesis limitations of using HuBERT semantic tokens paired with a standard HiFi-GAN detokenizer.
Minor clarity issues in Section 3.2 regarding the dimensionality mapping of the ungrouping mechanism and how the sizes in Equations 3, 4, and 5 reconcile.

strengths: Innovative dual-resolution speech representation (DRSR) design that compresses the LLM's input/output audio rate to 5Hz, dramatically reducing computational costs (by nearly 50% GPU hours) and resolving the text-speech token rate mismatch.
The introduction of the Speech Refined Head (SRH) enables high-quality, fine-grained 25Hz audio generation despite the low-frequency 5Hz backbone LLM representation.

Practical training strategies: CoM-Mixing (Chain-of-Modality) allows the model to flexibly perform text, direct speech-text, or reasoning-based cascaded generation, while the Core-Cocktail training (model merging) successfully prevents the degradation of base LLM textual capabilities.

Strong and comprehensive experimental results on multiple competitive speech benchmarks (OpenAudioBench, VoiceBench, UltraEval-Audio, Big Bench Audio), outperforming or being on par with strong recent open-source baselines like Qwen2.5-Omni and Kimi-Audio.
weaknesses: The speech-to-text alignment (ASR-WER) of 11.2 is slightly worse than some top baselines like Qwen2.5-Omni (3.48), suggesting that the textual guidance of the hidden states in SRH could be further improved by explicitly conditioning on text tokens as noted in the limitations.

The architecture and training details of the Speech Refined Head (SRH) could be more thoroughly explained. For instance, more details on the exact model size, layers, and structure of SRH (which is initialized from a pre-trained TTS model) would improve reproducibility.

The Core-Cocktail training strategy adds a degree of complexity with its two-stage fine-tuning and parameter merging steps, which might make the training pipeline harder to tune than single-stage end-to-end approaches.

strengths: The proposed Dual-Resolution Speech Representations (DRSR) mechanism is highly practical, successfully reducing the input-output sequence frame rate processed by the LLM backbone to 5Hz while preserving generation quality. This significantly improves training and inference efficiency.

The paper introduces two robust training strategies: CoM-Mixing (Chain-of-Modality) to support multiple interactive patterns, and the Core-Cocktail training strategy, which effectively addresses the training optimization dilemma and prevents the degradation of the base LLM's text capabilities.

Comprehensive experimental results show that DRVOICE-7B achieves state-of-the-art performance on OpenAudioBench and Big Bench Audio, while maintaining competitive results on VoiceBench and UltraEval-Audio.
The ablation studies are thorough and systematically analyze the impact of each module (CSE, SRH, CoM, and grouping factor) as well as the effects of data scaling and training datasets.
weaknesses: Although the backbone LLM operates at a lower frame rate (5Hz), the Speech Refined Head (SRH) still requires sequential autoregressive generation of $k$ tokens per step (where $k=5$). The paper lacks a concrete latency analysis (such as Real-Time Factor, RTF, or time-to-first-token comparison) to demonstrate the actual speedups in practice.

The speech-text alignment (ASR-WER of 11.2 in Table 3) is relatively weak compared to top-performing models like Qwen2.5-Omni (3.48), indicating that the lack of direct text conditioning in the speech generator head limits fine-grained text-to-speech alignment.
The reliance on external, pre-trained modules (like S3Tokenizer, CosyVoice, and HiFi-GAN) means the acoustic details and speech quality heavily depend on these frozen upstream components.

strengths: Strong Motivation and Efficiency: Proposes a practical solution (Dual-Resolution Speech Representations) to address the high computational costs and token-rate mismatch in joint speech-text autoregressive modeling. Bringing the internal LLM frame rate down to 5Hz while keeping 25Hz generation quality is a valuable contribution.

Impressive Empirical Results: Outperforms or achieves competitive performance against strong, established baselines (such as Qwen2.5-Omni, MiniCPM-o, Kimi-Audio) on major benchmarks including OpenAudioBench, VoiceBench, UltraEval-Audio, and Big Bench Audio.

Thorough Ablation Studies: The paper provides detailed ablations on almost all proposed components (SRH, grouping factors, continuous speech encoder, CoM-mixing, training stages), backed by concrete statistics on GPU training hours.
Well-designed Training Paradigms: The Core-Cocktail training strategy and CoM-mixing are clever ways to combat the forgetting of textual reasoning capabilities in speech-instruction tuning.
weaknesses: Incremental Novelty of Components: Some individual components are heavily borrowed or adapted from prior works. For instance, the Core-Cocktail training is directly derived from LM-Cocktail (Xiao et al., 2024), and CoM is from SpeechGPT (Zhang et al., 2023a). While the integration is effective, the conceptual novelty of these modules is somewhat limited.

Reliance on Model-Based Audio Evaluation: The voice quality is evaluated primarily using UTMOS, which is a neural-network-based MOS predictor. Given that the paper proposes a new Speech Refined Head for generation, a subjective human Mean Opinion Score (MOS) study would make the claim of high-quality speech generation much more convincing.

Attribution of Speech Quality: The speech generation uses S3Tokenizer tokens which are then synthesized via CosyVoice's Flow Matching decoder. It is not entirely clear how much of the speech naturalness/quality is due to the proposed DRVoice model's token generation versus the powerful underlying zero-shot TTS capabilities of CosyVoice.

Clarity of Figure 1: The schematic diagram in Figure 1 is quite dense. The precise mechanism of the Speech Refined Head (SRH) doing "k autoregressive forward passes" could be visualized or explained more clearly in the main text to help readers easily grasp how the grouping factor of $k$ is handled during parallel generation.
